textRun.content: You will complete three short tasks today: a word search, a general knowledge quiz, and a pattern logic task. Please work quickly and accurately without using any outside resources (no web searches, notes, or calculators). One of the three tasks will be randomly selected to determine a performance-based bonus; higher performance on that task earns you a larger bonus.

On the next page you’ll see one example with a solution for each task so you can familiarize yourself with the format. The examples are not scored. After the examples, the real tasks begin and each is timed. Once a timer ends, the page will advance automatically and you cannot go back, so please keep an eye on the time.

You will complete three word-search puzzles. You have 90 seconds per puzzle. Each puzzle contains 10 hidden target words, and you will see a list of 30 candidate words below the grid. Check every candidate you believe appears in the grid; leave unchecked any you believe do not.

Your score for this task is based on correct minus incorrect selections, and the task total cannot be negative (so random clicking is discouraged). When the timer ends, the page will move on automatically.

You will answer 48 multiple-choice questions in 4 minutes. Questions cover a mix of topics (e.g., geography, arts, history) and appear in random order. Each question has four options with one correct answer. If you don’t know an answer, make your best guess before time runs out.

You will solve 10 visual pattern problems. Each problem shows a 3×3 matrix with one cell missing. Choose the option (from six possibilities) that best completes the pattern. You have 5 minutes for this task, so work steadily and guess if you’re unsure.

You are an endorser for [ORGANIZATION 1: Vertex].

Each candidate set has two candidates: one from [ORGANIZATION 1: Vertex] (your organization's candidate) and one from [ORGANIZATION 2: Beacon]. You will see the available quiz and word search performance information for both candidates.

Your task is to set your endorsement strength for your organization's candidate. You are not choosing between the two candidates: you always endorse the [ORGANIZATION 1: Vertex] candidate. [Design notes: must-endorse resolution of the May 30 fork. Unipolar 0-100 strength slider replaces the bipolar A/B slider (bipolar was premised on free choice); anchors 0 = Weakest endorsement, 100 = Strongest endorsement. Raw strength maps to the 10-90 display range via displayConfidence(raw), so the display pipeline and the q2_strength_delta control are unchanged. Own-org candidate card always shown first. Evaluators (participants in a separate study) review your endorsements. For each one, they see your organization, the candidate you endorsed, and your endorsement strength.

They decide what percent of a $0.50 bank (0-100%) to wager on your endorsement being correct. At the end of their session, they decide how much future review to allocate to you and to your organization.

Your earnings: $1 for completing the study, plus a bonus of up to $3. One of your endorsements is picked at random, along with one evaluator who reviewed it. Your bonus for that endorsement has three parts:

1. Candidate performance. You start with a $0.50 bank, and your endorsement strength works like a wager. Your candidate wins if they score higher on the logical reasoning test than the other organization's candidate in that set, and loses if they score lower. Win: $0.50 plus ($0.50 times your strength percentage). Lose: $0.50 minus ($0.50 times your strength percentage). At strength 80: $0.90 if your candidate wins, $0.10 if your candidate loses.
2. Evaluator trust. If your candidate wins, you also earn $1.00 times the evaluator's wager percentage, up to $1.00.

3. Evaluator allocations. At the end of their session, the evaluator allocates 0 to 10 future review slots to you and 0 to 10 to your organization. Each of those 20 possible slots adds $0.05, up to $1.00 total across both, paid whether your candidate wins or loses.

Fielded-study opening: In this study, you will review real endorsement decisions made by another participant. Your decisions are real: they determine your own bonus and can affect that participant's pay.
You will see another participant's real endorsement decisions and decide how much of your own compensation to wager on whether those endorsements were correct.
Candidates: earlier participants who completed three tasks, a word-search puzzle, a general-knowledge quiz, and a logical-reasoning test.

Endorsers: a separate group, each assigned to represent an organization. Each decision showed an endorser two candidates, one from their own organization and one from another organization, plus the available quiz and word-search scores for those candidates. The endorser did not choose between the candidates. They had to endorse their own organization's candidate, and chose only how strongly to endorse. Their endorsement strength showed how confident they were that their candidate would score higher on the logical-reasoning test than the other organization's candidate in the same set.

Your task is to judge how much you trust one endorser. You will see a subset of their real decisions, not necessarily in the order they were made. Each one shows the endorser's organization, the endorsed candidate (always from the endorser's own organization), and the endorsement strength they set, which is how strongly they backed that candidate. You will not see the candidates' performance information. You then wager part of your own compensation on whether the endorsement was correct.

Endorsers had real incentives to endorse carefully. Their pay works like a wager: a stronger endorsement earns more if their candidate scores higher on the logical-reasoning test than the other organization's candidate in that set, and earns less if their candidate scores lower.

Their pay also depends on you. If their candidate wins, the more you wager, the larger their bonus. And at the end of this session, you will allocate future review slots to this endorser and to their organization; each slot you allocate adds to their bonus, whether their candidate won or lost.

For this endorser's payment, one endorsement and one evaluator who reviewed it are selected at random. If your session is selected, your wager on that endorsement and your allocations directly determine part of this endorser's pay.

You will evaluate three decisions made by the same endorser, each with a new, independent set of candidates. For each decision, you start with a $0.50 bank and choose what percent of it (0-100%) to wager on the endorser being correct. Your dollar wager is $0.50 times the percent you choose.
If the endorser was right, you get your $0.50 plus your dollar wager.
If the endorser was wrong, you get your $0.50 minus your dollar wager.
For example, say you wager 10% (which is $0.05 of your $0.50):
Wagering 0% means you keep your $0.50 no matter what. Wagering 100% means you could earn $1.00 or $0.00.

An endorsement is correct if the endorsed candidate scored higher on the logical-reasoning test than the other organization's candidate in the same set. Your bonus from these three decisions is the sum of all three (up to $3.00). You will find out whether the endorser was right immediately after each wager.

decisions made by prior participants who acted as
are people (not the endorsers) who previously completed three tasks: a logical-reasoning test, a general-knowledge quiz, and a word-search puzzle.

Endorsers learned how two candidates performed on the knowledge and word-search tasks and then used a slider to predict which candidate would score higher on the logical-reasoning task. Each endorser made predictions for multiple candidate sets.

You will evaluate a random subset of endorsements made by one or two prior participants. This means that you will be shown multiple endorsements made by the same endorser. These endorsement decisions will be randomly selected from the entire set of the endorser’s decisions (meaning, you may not be seeing the endorser’s decisions in chronological order). For each evaluation, you will see the endorser’s slider position (0–100). Positions closer to 0 indicate the endorser favored Candidate A; positions closer to 100 indicate the endorser favored Candidate B; distance from 50 reflects the endorser’s confidence.

Your task is to indicate what percentage of your own bonus (0%–100%) you wish to stake on the endorser’s prediction being correct. An endorsement is correct if the candidate favored by the endorser scores higher on the logical-reasoning task than the other candidate. You will find out the outcome of each of your bets in real time, meaning that after each decision you make, you will find out immediately whether the candidate you favored was, in fact, the better performer on the logic-based reasoning task.
After all decisions are complete, one of your evaluation decisions will be randomly selected to determine your bonus payment.
Your bonus is based on whether you bet on the right candidate.
Specifically, you can earn a bonus of up to $2. For each set of candidates, you will use

a slider to select any value from 0 to 100 percent, indicating how much you want to bet on the endorsed candidate winning.  If the endorser correctly predicted the better performer, your bonus equals $2 multiplied by your stake percentage. If the endorser incorrectly predicted the better performer, your bonus equals $2 multiplied by 100 minus your stake percent.

Note that endorsers are motivated to provide accurate predictions, because their payment amount depends on the accuracy of their prediction. Moreover, the more you bet on an accurate endorsement, the higher the endorser’s bonus. The lower the amount you bet on their endorsement, the less money the endorser will earn, even if their prediction ends up being correct. In other words, endorsers’ bonuses depend both on their accuracy and on your willingness to bet on them.
